title: Nomenclature
description: Read a structure, identify the principal group, and assemble an unambiguous name.

sources.label: IUPAC Blue Book P-14.5.1–2: simple and compound substituent ordering (inspected 2026-10-19)

review.note: Source-backed author review; not independently expert-verified.

lessons.label: Parent Chains
lessons.title: 1.1 Parent Chains, Locant Tiebreakers & Alphabetization
lessons.tag: Principal Group → Longest Chain → Lowest Locants

cards.rule: For the simple saturated acyclic structures here, choose the longest continuous carbon chain; tied lengths favor more substituents. For functionalized structures, first include the principal suffix group and required unsaturation. Compare locant sets at their first difference, not by their sum.
cards.cue:
Alphabetize substituent names: Ignore locants and multipliers that count repeated simple substituents: dimethyl is ordered under m. In traditional alkyl names, ignore n-, sec-, and tert-; include iso-, neo-, and cyclo- when part of the substituent name (isopropyl under i; cyclopropyl under c). The parent name is not part of this substituent list.
For a compound substituent in parentheses, use its complete name: (1,1-dimethylethyl) is ordered under d. A multiplier within that substituent is retained for alphabetization.
cards.trap:
The "Fake Parent Chain" Trap ("2,3-diethylpentane"):
An ethyl group at C2 of a pentane chain extends the longest chain to 6 carbons (3-ethyl-4-methylhexane). Always draw out suspect names!
cards.app:
Branched Amino Acids (Val, Leu, Ile):
Recognizing isopropyl (Valine), isobutyl (Leucine), and sec-butyl (Isoleucine) lets you classify hydrophobic side chains on sight.

steps.label: 1. Inspect
steps.text: Step 1 (Inspect): Unnumbered hydrocarbon with 11 total carbons. Trace every continuous path before choosing the parent chain.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom assigned Carbon #1 in this structure!
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbon G (right end) is C1 because right-to-left gives locants (2,3,4) instead of left-to-right (4,5,6).

steps.label: 2. Parent Chain
steps.text: Step 2 (Longest Chain + Tiebreaker): The longest continuous path has 7 carbons (heptane). Going through the ethyl branch only reaches 6 carbons, so the 7-carbon path wins. (If two chains did tie, pick the one with more substituents.)

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom assigned Carbon #1 in this structure!
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbon G (right end) is C1 because right-to-left gives locants (2,3,4) instead of left-to-right (4,5,6).

steps.label: 3. Number Carbons
steps.text: Step 3 (Animated Carbon Numbering): Numbering right-to-left gives (2,3,4); left-to-right gives (4,5,6). Compare at the first point of difference: 2 < 4.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom assigned Carbon #1 in this structure!
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbon G (right end) is C1 because right-to-left gives locants (2,3,4) instead of left-to-right (4,5,6).

steps.label: 4. Assemble Name
steps.text: Step 4 (IUPAC Name Assembly): Alphabetize 4-ethyl before 2,3-dimethyl (ignore di-) → 4-ethyl-2,3-dimethylheptane.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom assigned Carbon #1 in this structure!
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbon G (right end) is C1 because right-to-left gives locants (2,3,4) instead of left-to-right (4,5,6).

rule.title: 4-Step IUPAC Hierarchy: Suffix → Chain → First Point of Difference → Alphabetical

items.label: Principal Functional Group
items.text: Highest-priority group sets the suffix (-oic acid, -al, -one, -ol) and gets the lowest possible locant.

items.label: Longest Carbon Chain
items.text: Find the longest continuous carbon chain containing the principal functional group and maximum unsaturation.

items.label: First Point of Difference
items.text: Number from the end that gives the lower number at the very first locant difference (e.g., 2,3,6 beats 2,5,6).

items.label: Alphabetical Tiebreaker
items.text: If locant sets are identical from both ends, give the lower locant to the substituent that comes first alphabetically.

figure.caption: Parent-chain path and locants on an illustrative branched skeleton.

cue.title: Alphabetization Prefix Rule: Ignore di-, tri-, sec-, tert-; Keep iso-, neo-, cyclo-
cue.prompt: Which prefix type are you alphabetizing in an IUPAC name?

items.label: di- / tri- / tetra-
items.text: Multiplicative prefixes only count how many identical groups exist: "ethyl" comes before "dimethyl" (e vs m).

items.label: sec- / tert-
items.text: Ignore sec- and tert- in alphabetization; retain iso-, neo- and cyclo-. Alphabetize the complete substituent name for compound substituents.

items.label: iso- / neo- / cyclo-
items.text: Non-hyphenated structural prefixes are part of the base group name: "isopropyl" is alphabetized under I, "cyclopropyl" under C.

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

trap.title: Sum-of-Locants Myth vs. First Point of Difference

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Adding up all locants ("sum of locants") or alphabetizing "dimethyl" under D before "ethyl" under E.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Compare locant sets left-to-right at the first point of difference (2,3,6 < 2,5,6), and alphabetize "ethyl" (E) before "dimethyl" (M).

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

app.title: Reconstructing Unfamiliar Drug & Metabolite Structures on MCAT Passages

items.label: Passage Stem
items.text: Parse the proposed name, then redraw and verify the longest eligible chain before accepting it.

items.label: Chain & Suffix
items.text: The longest eligible parent must include the aldehyde carbon; a longer path that omits C1 cannot replace it.

items.label: Branch Verification
items.text: The proposed 2-ethyl-4,4-dimethylpentanal has a five-carbon parent containing the aldehyde carbon. The six-carbon path through the ethyl branch omits that required carbon.

cards.rule: An alcohol (–OH) has higher IUPAC naming seniority than carbon–carbon double or triple bonds. Replace the final –e with –ol and number the chain to give the –OH carbon the lowest possible locant.
cards.cue:
Infix + Suffix Pattern (Root + en/yn + ol):
Unsaturation inside the parent chain stays in the stem as –en– or –yn– (e.g., but-3-en-2-ol).
cards.trap: Give the principal alcohol the lowest locant before the C=C or C≡C. If multiple-bond locant sets tie in an enyne, the double bond receives the lower locant.
cards.app:
Common Alcohol Names:
Ethanol = ethyl alcohol; propan-2-ol (2-propanol) = isopropyl alcohol. Subordinate –OH is named hydroxy–.

steps.label: 1. Inspect
steps.text: Step 1 (Inspect): Unnumbered skeletal structure. Identify the alcohol (–OH) and the double bond (C=C).

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom that must be Carbon #1 in this unsaturated alcohol!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon D (right end) is C1 so the principal alcohol group gets locant 2 instead of 3.

steps.label: 2. Principal Group
steps.text: Step 2 (Identify Principal Group): By IUPAC seniority, alcohols (–OH) outrank alkenes and alkynes and supply the suffix –ol.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom that must be Carbon #1 in this unsaturated alcohol!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon D (right end) is C1 so the principal alcohol group gets locant 2 instead of 3.

steps.label: 3. Parent Chain
steps.text: Step 3 (Parent Chain & Infix): Both the –OH carbon and C=C bond lie in the 4-carbon chain, so C=C becomes the infix –en–.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom that must be Carbon #1 in this unsaturated alcohol!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon D (right end) is C1 so the principal alcohol group gets locant 2 instead of 3.

steps.label: 4. Number & Name
steps.text: Step 4 (Number & Assemble): Right-to-left gives –OH locant 2 (rather than 3). The double bond starts at C3 → but-3-en-2-ol.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom that must be Carbon #1 in this unsaturated alcohol!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon D (right end) is C1 so the principal alcohol group gets locant 2 instead of 3.

rule.title: Alcohol Suffix (-ol) Outranks All C–C Multiple Bonds & Halide/Alkyl Substituents

items.label: Alcohol (-ol) Priority
items.text: Outranks alkenes (-ene), alkynes (-yne), halides, and alkyl chains; always number to give -ol the lowest locant.

items.label: Combined Enol / Ynol Names
items.text: Keep unsaturation in the stem and attach -ol at the end: e.g., pent-3-en-1-ol (drop terminal "e" before vowel).

items.label: Alkene vs. Alkyne Locant Rule
items.text: Lowest locant set for all multiple bonds wins first; only if tied (e.g., 1,6 vs 1,6) does alkene (-en-) beat alkyne (-yn-).

figure.caption: Principal OH and unsaturation on the same molecular graph.

cue.title: Suffix vs. Prefix Switch for -OH Groups
cue.prompt: Is the alcohol (-OH) the highest-priority group in the molecule?

items.label: Yes — Highest Priority
items.text: Alcohol dominates the parent chain numbering over alkenes, alkynes, halides, and alkyls (e.g., but-3-en-1-ol).

items.label: No — Carbonyl/Acid Present
items.text: When a carboxylic acid, ester, aldehyde, or ketone is present, -OH becomes a substituent (e.g., 3-hydroxybutanal).

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

trap.title: Giving Alkene C=C a Lower Locant Than Alcohol -OH

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Naming HO–CH₂–CH₂–CH=CH₂ as "but-1-en-4-ol" to give the double bond C1.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Name it "but-3-en-1-ol": the principal suffix (-ol) always outranks carbon-carbon unsaturation.

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

app.title: Terpene Alcohols, Retinol & Steroid Suffixes (-ol vs -one)

items.label: Retinol / Geraniol
items.text: The -ol suffix immediately tells you the alcohol is the highest-priority group and C1 is anchored near -OH.

items.label: Estradiol vs. Estrone
items.text: Suffix shifts instantly reveal whether a steroid hormone carries alcohol or ketone functionality.

items.label: Enol Intermediates
items.text: Recognize enols as transient tautomers that rapidly rearrange to more stable carbonyls.

cards.rule: A senior suffix such as –ol determines the starting locant first. In a simple cycloalkene with no senior suffix, the double bond occupies C1 and C2. Then minimize substituent locants at the first difference; use alphabetization only for a remaining appropriate tie.
cards.cue:
"Never Jump Across a Ring Double Bond!"
If you assign one alkene carbon C1, C2 must be the other carbon of that double bond.
cards.trap:
Why "Most Substituted Carbon First" Fails:
In 4-propylcyclohexene, the alkene takes C1–C2 priority over the propyl substituent. Only use substitution when priority tiers tie (1,1,2-trimethylcyclobutane beats 1,2,2-).
cards.app: Ring recognition helps interpret cyclic biomolecules. Retinal is an aldehyde related to vitamin A. Steroids use established fused-ring parent numbering; do not extend simple cyclohexene numbering mechanically to steroid skeletons.

steps.label: 1. Inspect Ring
steps.text: Step 1 (Inspect): A 6-membered ring with a double bond, a methyl group on one alkene carbon, and an ethyl group across the ring.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the ring carbon that must be assigned Carbon #1!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon E is C1 because numbering clockwise through the double bond (E=C1 → F=C2 → A=C3 → B=C4) gives substituent locants (1,4) instead of (2,5)!

steps.label: 2. Lock C1–C2 on C=C
steps.text: Step 2 (Cycloalkene Rule): Unsaturation outranks alkyl substituents, so the two carbons of the double bond must be C1 and C2.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the ring carbon that must be assigned Carbon #1!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon E is C1 because numbering clockwise through the double bond (E=C1 → F=C2 → A=C3 → B=C4) gives substituent locants (1,4) instead of (2,5)!

steps.label: 3. Number & Name
steps.text: Step 3 (Compare Locant Sets): Clockwise from the methylated alkene carbon (E=C1 → F=C2 → A=C3 → B=C4) gives substituent locants (1,4), beating counter-clockwise (2,5) → 4-ethyl-1-methylcyclohex-1-ene.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the ring carbon that must be assigned Carbon #1!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon E is C1 because numbering clockwise through the double bond (E=C1 → F=C2 → A=C3 → B=C4) gives substituent locants (1,4) instead of (2,5)!

rule.title: Ring Numbering: C1 at Principal Group/Double Bond → Minimize Next Substituent Locant

items.label: Anchor C1 at Principal Group
items.text: In cycloalkanols or cycloalkanones, C1 is automatically the carbon bearing -OH or =O.

items.label: Cycloalkene Double Bond Walk
items.text: In cycloalkenes, C1 and C2 MUST step across the double bond; choose the direction that gives the first substituent the lowest locant.

items.label: Polysubstituted Cycloalkanes
items.text: Start at the carbon that yields the lowest locant set (e.g., 1,1,3 beats 1,3,3); break ties alphabetically.

figure.caption: Trace the ring across its double bond before resolving substituent locants.

cue.title: Ring vs. Open Chain: Which One Is the Parent?
cue.prompt: How do you choose between a ring and an attached chain as the parent?

items.label: Cycloalkene without senior suffix
items.text: Assign the two alkene carbons 1 and 2, then minimize substituent locants.

items.label: Senior suffix present
items.text: A principal alcohol or other senior suffix controls numbering; do not force its carbon to also be an alkene carbon.

trap.title: Stepping Away from C1=C2 in Cycloalkenes

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Numbering C1 at one alkene carbon and stepping away from the double bond to hit a methyl group at C2.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: In cycloalkenes, C1 and C2 MUST be the two carbons of the double bond (e.g., 3-methylcyclohex-1-ene, never 2-methyl).

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

items.label: Menthol Scaffold
items.text: C1 is fixed at -OH; numbering proceeds toward C2 isopropyl (1,2,5 < 1,3,6).

items.label: Cycloalkene Intermediates
items.text: Used to track regioselective hydroboration or epoxidation sites on cyclic substrates.

items.label: Bicyclic / Steroid Rings
items.text: Fixed numbering lets passages reference C3-OH or C17-ketone without ambiguity.

lessons.label: Diols & Hydrates
lessons.title: 1.4 Geminal vs. Vicinal Diols & Reversible Hydration

cards.rule: Alcohols with two hydroxyl groups are named alkane-x,y-diols (preserving the –e of the parent alkane before "d"). Every hydroxyl gets a locant number.
cards.cue:
Memory cue:
• Vicinal = in the vicinity (adjacent carbons, 1,2).
• Geminal = Gemini twins (same carbon, 1,1).
cards.trap: Carbonyl hydration is reversible. Electron-withdrawing substituents and less crowding generally favor the hydrate. Formaldehyde is strongly hydrated in water; acetone predominantly remains a carbonyl. The equilibrium depends on conditions.
cards.app: In aqueous aldehyde oxidation, the hydrated form can participate in oxidation to the carboxylic acid. Hydration and oxidation are distinct steps.

steps.label: 1. Vicinal Diol (1,2)
steps.text: Vicinal Diol (Glycol): Two –OH groups on adjacent carbons: ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol).

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click both carbon atoms bearing hydroxyl groups in this vicinal diol!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Both adjacent carbons (C1 and C2) carry hydroxyl groups in ethane-1,2-diol.

steps.label: 2. Geminal Diol (1,1)
steps.text: Geminal Diol (Hydrate): Two –OH groups on the same carbon (propane-2,2-diol), in reversible equilibrium with a carbonyl + H₂O.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the single carbon atom bearing BOTH hydroxyl groups in this geminal diol!
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbon B (C2) carries both hydroxyl groups in propane-2,2-diol.

rule.title: Geminal 1,1-diols and vicinal 1,2-diols: connectivity and hydration equilibrium
rule.formula: R₂C=O + H₂O ⇌ R₂C(OH)₂   (K_eq ≪ 1 for most ketones; K_eq > 1 for H₂C=O or Cl₃C–CHO)

items.label: Geminal Diol (1,1)
items.text: Two -OH groups on the SAME carbon; spontaneously loses H₂O to form a carbonyl (C=O σ+π is stronger than two C–O σ bonds).

items.label: Vicinal Diol (1,2)
items.text: Two -OH groups on ADJACENT carbons; stable, isolable glycol formed from alkene dihydroxylation (OsO₄) or epoxide opening.

chips: Hydration depends on structure and conditions

figure.caption: Compare adjacent-carbon and same-carbon OH groups; distinct illustrative structures.

cue.title: Mnemonic: "GEM = Twins on ONE Carbon; VIC = Neighbors in the VICinity"
cue.prompt: What kind of diol or carbonyl substrate do you see?

items.label: 1,1-Diol (Geminal)
items.text: Treat a 1,1-diol as a disguised carbonyl hydrate in aqueous equilibrium.

items.label: 1,2-Diol (Vicinal)
items.text: Stable to water loss; undergoes oxidative C–C cleavage with periodate (NaIO₄) or pinacol rearrangement in strong acid.

items.label: Aldehyde + Adjacent EWGs
items.text: Strong electron-withdrawing groups (–CCl₃, –CF₃) destabilize the δ+ carbonyl carbon, favoring the sp³ gem-diol.

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

trap.title: Dropping the Vowel "e" Before "-diol" or Isolating Simple Gem-Diols

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Writing "ethandiol" (dropping the "e") or assuming propan-2,2-diol can be bottled as a pure liquid.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Retain the "e" before consonant suffix "-diol" (ethane-1,2-diol), and recognize that simple 1,1-diols revert to ketones/aldehydes.

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

app.title: Serine Protease Tetrahedral Intermediates & Periodate Sugar Cleavage

items.label: Chloral Hydrate
items.text: Three inductive Cl atoms make the aldehyde carbonyl so electrophilic that the geminal diol predominates in water.

items.label: Carbonic Anhydrase / CO₂
items.text: Hydration of CO₂ is biologically analogous to reversible carbonyl hydration.

items.label: Carbohydrate Vicinal Diols
items.text: Periodate (IO₄⁻) selectively cleaves vicinal diols in sugar rings to determine ring size.

cards.rule: Aldehydes have a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one H; ketones have two carbon substituents. The simple acyclic examples here use –al and –one. A formyl group attached to a ring may instead require a –carbaldehyde name. Subordinate carbonyl naming depends on whether its carbon belongs to the selected parent; oxo– and formyl– are not universally interchangeable.
cards.trap:
Acetone Carbon-Count Trap:
Although acet– usually means 2 carbons, acetone (propanone) has 3 carbons because a ketone requires a carbon on both sides of C=O!
cards.app:
Aldoses, Ketoses & Enolates:
Carbohydrates are aldoses or ketoses; acidic α-hydrogens on α-carbons form nucleophilic enolates in aldol reactions.

steps.label: 1. Inspect Carbonyl
steps.text: Step 1 (Classify): C=O bonded to two carbons is an internal ketone (–one); terminal C=O bonded to H is an aldehyde (–al).

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click BOTH α-carbons in pentan-2-one! (Do not click the C=O carbon).
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbons A (C1) and C (C3) are directly adjacent to C2=O, making both α-carbons!

steps.label: 2. Number Ketone
steps.text: Step 2 (Numbering): Left-to-right gives C=O C2 (rather than C4).

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click BOTH α-carbons in pentan-2-one! (Do not click the C=O carbon).
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbons A (C1) and C (C3) are directly adjacent to C2=O, making both α-carbons!

steps.label: 3. α-Carbons & Name
steps.text: Step 3 (Greek Letters & Name): Carbons directly adjacent to C=O are α-carbons (C1 and C3), followed by β (C4) and γ (C5) → pentan-2-one.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click BOTH α-carbons in pentan-2-one! (Do not click the C=O carbon).
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbons A (C1) and C (C3) are directly adjacent to C2=O, making both α-carbons!

steps.label: 4. Aldehyde Priority
steps.text: Step 4 (4-hydroxybutanal): Terminal aldehyde outranks alcohol, taking C1 (–al) while the C4 alcohol becomes 4-hydroxy–.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom that must be assigned Carbon #1 in this hydroxy aldehyde!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon D (the aldehyde carbon on the right) outranks the alcohol and is automatically C1.

rule.title: Aldehydes (-al) Outrank Ketones (-one); Greek Letters (α, β, γ) Start Adjacent to C=O

items.label: Aldehyde (-al) Priority
items.text: Terminal R–CHO defines C1 (locant 1 omitted in simple chains: butanal). Ring-attached –CHO is "-carbaldehyde".

items.label: Ketone (-one) Numbering
items.text: Internal R–CO–R′ requires a locant in chains ≥5 carbons (pentan-2-one vs pentan-3-one); becomes "oxo-" when outranked.

items.label: Greek Letter Mapping (α, β, γ)
items.text: The carbonyl carbon itself has NO Greek letter; α is the directly attached carbon, β is two bonds away, γ is three.

figure.caption: Separate ketone and hydroxy-aldehyde examples; this is not a reaction pair.

cue.title: Prefix Selection When Carbonyls Are Outranked: "oxo-" vs. "formyl-"
cue.prompt: How do you name a carbonyl when a higher-priority group (-COOH or ester) is present?

items.label: Ketone on Parent Chain
items.text: Example: 3-oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid) — ketone at C3 is outranked by C1 carboxylic acid.

items.label: Aldehyde Counted IN Parent Chain
items.text: Example: 4-oxobutanoic acid — the aldehyde carbon IS C4 of the 4-carbon chain.

items.label: –CHO Attached as a Pendant Branch
items.text: Used when the –CHO carbon cannot be included in the main parent chain or ring.

trap.title: Calling the Carbonyl Carbon "α" or Mixing Up Greek Letters with IUPAC Numbers

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Labeling the C=O carbon as the α-carbon or writing "2-α-methylbutanal" in a systematic name.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: C=O is the reference point (C1 in aldehydes); C2 is the α-carbon, C3 is the β-carbon, and never mix Greek letters into IUPAC numbering.

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

app.title: Ketone Bodies (Acetoacetate) & Pyridoxal Phosphate (PLP) Schiff Bases

items.label: Acetoacetate (Ketone Body)
items.text: The ketone sits at the β-carbon (C3) relative to the C1 carboxylate, enabling facile decarboxylation to acetone.

items.label: Aldolase Substrates
items.text: Deprotonation at the α-carbon forms the nucleophile that attacks a partner aldehyde C=O.

items.label: Retinal & PLP Cofactors
items.text: Terminal aldehyde reacts with lysine ε-NH₂ to form a conjugated imine linkage.

lessons.label: Acids & Priority
lessons.title: 1.6 Carboxylic Acids, Derivatives & Master Priority Hierarchy
lessons.tag: Acid > Anhydride > Ester > Amide > Aldehyde > Ketone > Alcohol

cards.rule: For these examples, naming seniority is acid > anhydride > ester > amide > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol. Naming seniority is a convention, not an oxidation-state calculation. Unsaturation is retained in the parent name. This is a chapter subset, not the complete IUPAC hierarchy.
cards.cue:
Common Acid Roots:
• 1C: Formic acid (methanoic) → methyl formate
• 2C: Acetic acid (ethanoic) → acetic anhydride
• 3C: Propionic acid (propanoic)
cards.trap:
High-Yield Distinctions:
• Ester vs. Ether: Esters have C=O next to O; ethers (R–O–R′) do not.
• NADH Trap: NADH contains an amide (nicotinamide) and phosphoanhydride (P–O–P), NOT a carboxylic anhydride!
cards.app:
Pyruvic & Tartaric Acid:
• Pyruvic acid (acetylformic acid) = 2-oxopropanoic acid.
• Tartaric acid = 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid.

steps.label: 1. Multifunctional Acid
steps.text: Priority Winner: Carboxylic acid takes C1 and –oic acid. Alphabetize 4-hydroxy– before 2-oxo– → 4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoic acid.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click the carbon atom assigned Carbon #1 in this multifunctional acid!
challenge.explanation: Spot on! Carbon E (the carboxylic acid carbon) is C1, placing oxo at C2 and hydroxy at C4.

steps.label: 2. Ester (alkyl –oate)
steps.text: Ester Naming: O-attached alkyl group first (ethyl) + 3C acid parent (propanoate) → ethyl propanoate.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click Carbon #1 of the acyl parent chain (propanoate) in this ester!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon C is the ester carbonyl carbon (C1 of the 3-carbon propanoate parent).

steps.label: 3. N-Amide (N– prefix)
steps.text: Amide Naming: Nitrogen groups use capital N– and are alphabetized → N-ethyl-N-methylpropanamide.

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click Carbon #1 of the acyl parent chain (propanamide) in this amide!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbon C is the amide carbonyl carbon (C1 of the 3-carbon propanamide parent).

steps.label: 4. Anhydrides
steps.text: Anhydride Naming: Two acyl groups bridged by O (ethanoic anhydride = acetic anhydride).

challenge.prompt: 🖐️ Try It Yourself: Click BOTH carbonyl carbon atoms in ethanoic anhydride!
challenge.explanation: Correct! Carbons B and D are the two acyl carbonyl carbons flanking the central bridging oxygen.

rule.title: Master IUPAC Priority Hierarchy: Carboxylic Acid > Derivative > Carbonyl > Alcohol > Amine > Alkene

items.label: Carboxylic Acid (-oic acid)
items.text: Top of the organic hierarchy; always defines C1 at the –COOH carbon (or uses "-carboxylic acid" on rings).

items.label: Carboxylic Acid Derivatives
items.text: Anhydride > Ester (-oate) > Acid Halide (-oyl halide) > Amide (-amide) > Nitrile (-nitrile).

items.label: Aldehydes & Ketones
items.text: Aldehyde (-al) > Ketone (-one); both become "oxo-" when a carboxylic acid or derivative is present.

items.label: Alcohols, Thiols & Amines
items.text: Alcohol (-ol) > Thiol (-thiol) > Amine (-amine); demoted to hydroxy-, sulfanyl-, and amino- prefixes.

figure.caption: Compare a multifunctional acid and an N-substituted amide; no reaction is implied.

cue.title: Naming Multifunctional Molecules & Ester / Amide Attachments
cue.prompt: What type of carboxylic acid derivative or multifunctional compound are you naming?

items.label: Ester (R–CO–OR′)
items.text: Group on single-bonded oxygen is word 1 (ethyl); acyl chain with C=O is word 2 (ethanoate → ethyl ethanoate).

items.label: Substituted Amide (R–CO–NR′R″)
items.text: Substituents on nitrogen get locant N- (e.g., N,N-dimethylmethanamide = DMF).

items.label: Nitrile (R–C≡N)
items.text: Keep terminal "e" before "-nitrile" (butanenitrile = 4 carbons total including C≡N); prefix is "cyano-" when outranked.

figure.caption: Illustrative graph focus from the corresponding walkthrough explanation; no transformation is implied.

trap.title: Swapping the Acyl Chain and Oxygen-Alkyl Group in Esters

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Naming CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ as "methyl propanoate" or forgetting to count the C≡N carbon in a nitrile chain.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Split the ester at the C–O single bond: the oxygen bears "ethyl" and the C=O chain has 2 carbons ("ethanoate") → ethyl ethanoate.

app.title: Amino Acids, Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic Acid) & β-Lactam Antibiotics

items.label: Canonical Amino Acids
items.text: Carboxylic acid (-oic acid) outranks the amine, so –NH₂ is named as the "2-amino" prefix at Cα.

items.label: GABA Neurotransmitter
items.text: C1 is the carboxylic acid; C2=α, C3=β, C4=γ bears the amino substituent.

items.label: Aspirin Scaffold
items.text: Carboxylic acid is the principal group (-benzoic acid), while the ester is an acetoxy substituent.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Click all 6 carbon atoms in the longest continuous parent chain.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbons A–F form the 6-carbon hexane chain; G is a methyl branch.
hints: Trace a continuous route between two terminal carbons without visiting any carbon twice.
The parent contains six carbons; at the branch point, follow the longer route and leave the short methyl arm outside the parent.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: Which numbering direction gives the methyl branch its lowest locant?
feedback: Correct! Left-to-right gives C3 instead of C4.
Right-to-left puts the methyl group at C4 instead of C3!
stages.explanation: Correct! Left-to-right gives C3 instead of C4.
hints: Keep the same parent chain and count the branch position from each end.
Compare locants 3 and 4; choose the direction with the smaller branch locant.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the complete IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Spot on! 3-methylhexane.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Format as [locant]-[substituent][parent root][suffix] with a hyphen between the number and letter.
Hint 2 (Structure): There is a methyl group at C3 on a 6-carbon alkane parent (hexane).

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Why is "2-ethyl-4-methylpentane" an invalid name for this structure?
options: The 2-carbon branch extends the longest continuous chain to 6 carbons (hexane)
It has 8 carbons in a straight chain
feedback: Correct! An "ethyl" group at C2 extends the parent chain to 6 carbons.
There are 8 total carbons, but a continuous chain cannot fork (longest path = 6 carbons).
stages.explanation: Correct! An "ethyl" group at C2 extends the parent chain to 6 carbons.
hints: A parent chain may turn at a branch; it does not have to follow the most horizontal line.
Include the two-carbon arm in a continuous six-carbon route. The proposed pentane parent is too short.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: Which locant set is lower for the two methyl substituents?
feedback: Correct! At the first point of difference, 2 < 3.
Right-to-left gives locants (3,5), which loses to (2,4) at the first point of difference!
stages.explanation: Correct! At the first point of difference, 2 < 3.
hints: List the methyl locants in increasing order for each numbering direction.
Compare (2,4) with (3,5) at the first differing entry; do not compare their sums.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the true IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Correct! 2,4-dimethylhexane.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Two identical substituents require two locants separated by a comma and the multiplier prefix di–.
Hint 2 (Structure): Two methyl groups sit at C2 and C4 on a 6-carbon hexane chain.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Which group has highest priority and supplies the principal suffix?
feedback: Priority Error: Alcohols have higher IUPAC seniority than alkenes.
Correct! Alcohol supplies –ol and alkene stays in the stem as –en–.
stages.explanation: Correct! Alcohol supplies –ol and alkene stays in the stem as –en–.
hints: Decide which characteristic group takes the principal suffix when an alcohol and an alkene are both present.
The hydroxyl group supplies -ol; the double bond is still represented by -en-.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: Click the carbon atom on the diagram that must be assigned Carbon #1.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon D (right end) gives –OH locant 2 instead of 3.
hints: Number the four-carbon parent from both ends and compare the hydroxyl locant first.
Start at the terminal carbon nearest the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, even though that gives the double bond a larger locant.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the complete systematic IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Excellent! but-3-en-2-ol.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Combine the carbon root, the unsaturation locant + infix (–en–), and the principal alcohol locant + suffix (–ol).
Hint 2 (Structure): 4-carbon root (but), double bond starting at C3, and alcohol at C2.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Which group determines the principal suffix in this 5-carbon structure?
options: The alcohol (–ol; triple bond becomes –yn– infix)
feedback: Correct! Alcohols outrank alkynes.
Priority Error: Alcohols outrank both alkenes and alkynes.
stages.explanation: Correct! Alcohols outrank alkynes.
hints: An alkyne does not outrank an alcohol for the principal suffix.
Use -ol for the principal group and retain -yn- for the triple bond.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: Click the carbon atom that must be assigned Carbon #1.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon E (right end) gives the principal alcohol C2 instead of C4.
hints: Compare the hydroxyl position when the five-carbon chain is numbered from each end.
The end nearest the hydroxyl gives it locant 2 rather than 4; choose that end as C1.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the systematic IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Bravo! pent-4-yn-2-ol.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Use the triple-bond infix –yn– before the principal alcohol suffix –ol.
Hint 2 (Structure): 5-carbon chain (pent), triple bond at C4, and alcohol at C2.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Click the ring carbon that must be assigned Carbon #1.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon E is C1 because numbering clockwise through C1=C2 (E → F → A → B) gives substituent locants (1,4) instead of (2,5).
hints: In this cycloalkene, the two double-bond carbons receive locants 1 and 2.
Choose the alkene carbon bearing methyl as C1; this also lowers the substituent locants.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: With C1 at the methylated alkene carbon and C2 at the other alkene carbon, what is the ethyl locant?
feedback: Correct! Continuing clockwise from C1 through C2 places the ethyl group at C4; alphabetize 4-ethyl before 1-methyl.
(1,4) beats (2,5) at the first point of difference!
stages.explanation: Correct! Continuing clockwise from C1 through C2 places the ethyl group at C4; alphabetize 4-ethyl before 1-methyl.
hints: Follow the fixed C1-to-C2 direction around the ring to the ethyl attachment.
Count ring carbons only for the locant; the carbons inside the ethyl branch do not extend the ring numbering.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the complete IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Spot on! 4-ethyl-1-methylcyclohex-1-ene.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Alphabetize the substituents (ethyl before methyl), followed by the cycloalkene parent name.
Hint 2 (Structure): Ethyl is at C4 and methyl is at C1 on cyclohex-1-ene (or cyclohexene).

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Click the ring carbon that must be assigned Carbon #1.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon A bears the principal –OH group and is automatically C1.
hints: The hydroxyl group supplies the ring alcohol suffix.
The ring carbon directly bonded to oxygen receives locant 1.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: From C1 (at –OH), which direction gives the methyl group its lowest locant?
feedback: Correct! Clockwise gives C3 instead of counter-clockwise C5.
Counter-clockwise puts methyl at C5 instead of C3!
stages.explanation: Correct! Clockwise gives C3 instead of counter-clockwise C5.
hints: Keep the hydroxyl-bearing carbon at C1 and compare both routes around the ring.
Choose methyl at C3 rather than C5; the ring orientation on the page does not override the lower-locant rule.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the systematic IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Excellent! 3-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Prefix the methyl substituent and its locant before the cyclic alcohol parent name.
Hint 2 (Structure): Methyl at C3 on a cyclohexan-1-ol (or cyclohexanol) ring.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/2: How are the two hydroxyl groups positioned in this molecule?
options: Vicinal (on adjacent carbons C1 and C2)
feedback: Correct! Vicinal diols (glycols) have –OH on adjacent carbons.
Geminal diols have both –OH groups on the same carbon.
stages.explanation: Correct! Vicinal diols (glycols) have –OH on adjacent carbons.
hints: Find the carbon attached to each hydroxyl oxygen.
Hydroxyls on neighboring carbons are vicinal; hydroxyls on the same carbon are geminal.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/2: Type the systematic IUPAC name (common name: ethylene glycol).
stages.explanation: Correct! ethane-1,2-diol (retaining the final -e before -diol).
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Preserve the full alkane name (including –e) before adding the locants and –diol suffix.
Hint 2 (Structure): 2-carbon alkane (ethane) with hydroxyls at C1 and C2.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/2: Click the carbon atom bearing both hydroxyl groups in this geminal diol.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon B (C2) carries both –OH groups (formed by hydration of propanone/acetone).
hints: Follow both carbon–oxygen single bonds to their carbon endpoints.
Both hydroxyl oxygens connect to the central carbon of the three-carbon chain.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/2: Type the systematic IUPAC name (remember: every group needs a locant!).
stages.explanation: Spot on! propane-2,2-diol.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Even when both –OH groups sit on the same carbon, repeat the locant number before –diol.
Hint 2 (Structure): 3-carbon alkane (propane) with both hydroxyls at C2.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Click BOTH α-carbons on the diagram (do not click the C=O carbon).
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbons A and C flank the C=O carbon and are both α-carbons.
hints: An alpha carbon is directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon; the carbonyl carbon itself is excluded.
Find the C=O carbon, then select its two carbon neighbors, one on each side.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: Which direction gives the ketone carbonyl its lower locant?
feedback: Correct! C2 < C4.
Right-to-left gives the ketone C4 instead of C2!
stages.explanation: Correct! C2 < C4.
hints: Compare the carbonyl-carbon locant when counting from either end of the five-carbon chain.
The ketone receives locant 2 from one end and 4 from the other; choose the smaller value.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the systematic IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Spot on! pentan-2-one.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Replace the final –e of the alkane with the ketone locant and suffix –one.
Hint 2 (Structure): 5-carbon alkane (pentan-) with a ketone at C2.

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Click the carbon atom that must be assigned Carbon #1.
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon D is the terminal aldehyde carbon and is automatically C1.
hints: An aldehyde carbon belongs to the parent chain and outranks the alcohol for the suffix.
Select the carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to the explicitly drawn H; select the carbon, not that H.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: When an alcohol is subordinate to an aldehyde, how is the C4 –OH named?
feedback: Correct! Subordinate alcohols use the prefix hydroxy–.
oxo– is for subordinate carbonyls, not alcohols.
stages.explanation: Correct! Subordinate alcohols use the prefix hydroxy–.
hints: The aldehyde already supplies -al, so the alcohol must be expressed as a prefix.
Use hydroxy- with the hydroxyl-bearing carbon locant; do not add a second -ol suffix.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the complete IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Bravo! 4-hydroxybutanal.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Terminal aldehydes are assumed to be C1 and take the suffix –al without a number.
Hint 2 (Structure): 4-hydroxy prefix + 4-carbon aldehyde parent (butanal).

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Click the carbonyl carbon (Carbon #1 of the amide parent chain).
stages.explanation: Correct! Carbon C is C1 of the 3-carbon propanamide parent.
hints: The amide parent includes the carbonyl carbon; nitrogen-bound alkyl groups are named separately.
Choose the carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to nitrogen.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: How are the ethyl and methyl groups on nitrogen written?
feedback: Correct! Each N-group gets N– in alphabetical order.
Alphabetize ethyl before methyl.
stages.explanation: Correct! Each N-group gets N– in alphabetical order.
hints: Substituents attached directly to nitrogen use the letter locant N, not a parent-chain carbon number.
Give each nitrogen-bound group its own N locant and list ethyl before methyl alphabetically.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the complete IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Excellent! N-ethyl-N-methylpropanamide.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): List the alphabetized N-alkyl prefixes directly before the acyl parent amide name.
Hint 2 (Structure): N-ethyl-N-methyl + 3-carbon amide parent (propanamide).

stages.prompt: Stage 1/3: Which group has highest priority and determines the suffix?
feedback: Correct! Acid outranks ketone and alcohol.
Carboxylic acid outranks ketone.
stages.explanation: Correct! Acid outranks ketone and alcohol.
hints: Compare carboxylic acid, ketone, and alcohol naming seniority before choosing the suffix.
The carboxylic acid supplies -oic acid; the ketone and alcohol are named as prefixes.

stages.prompt: Stage 2/3: With C1 at the acid, what are the prefixes for the C2 ketone and C4 alcohol?
feedback: Correct! Alphabetized as 4-hydroxy-2-oxo–.
C1 is the acid on the right, so the ketone is C2 and the alcohol is C4!
stages.explanation: Correct! Alphabetized as 4-hydroxy-2-oxo–.
hints: With the acid fixed as C1, a subordinate ketone uses oxo- and a subordinate alcohol uses hydroxy-.
Attach 2 to oxo and 4 to hydroxy, then list the prefixes alphabetically.

stages.prompt: Stage 3/3: Type the complete IUPAC name.
stages.explanation: Bravo! 4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoic acid.
hints: Hint 1 (Rule): Alphabetize the prefixes ("h" in hydroxy before "o" in oxo) before the parent acid name.
Hint 2 (Structure): 4-hydroxy-2-oxo + 5-carbon carboxylic acid (pentanoic acid).
